clue.text: A king amid excited fans at palace quite unruffled

indicators.note: amid means set in the middle of, so the short pair sits inside the rearranged letters
excited fans are stirred up, so the letters of these three words are jumbled

parts.note: K is the chess and cards abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch among an animated crowd outside the palace stays perfectly calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Something completely flat has no bumps or ripples, so the idiom means entirely smooth, here figuratively calm.

clue.text: Tips from Tom Hanks in leading role, mainly

indicators.note: in tells us the tips are placed inside the phrase for the leading role

parts.note: the foremost part is the leading role in a play or film

indicators.note: the tips of words are their first letters, here of Tom and Hanks

explanation.surface: Tom Hanks has usually been the star of his films.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts TH, the tips of Tom and Hanks, into FOREMOST PART after its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday idiom for largely or on the whole, a synonym of the adverb.

clue.text: New dons loved wearing robes, perhaps

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the word for loved wears the letter for new around it

parts.note: adored means loved

explanation.surface: Freshly appointed university teachers enjoyed putting on their gowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like a noun for academics, but it is the verb: ADORED puts on N.
explanation.definitionFit: Adorned means decorated or dressed up; wearing ceremonial robes is one example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Mr Gore relies on retaining current benefactors

parts.note: Al Gore, the former US vice-president

indicators.note: retaining means holding within, so the verb's letters keep the current symbol inside

parts.note: trusts means relies on
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Al Gore depends on keeping up the flow, presumably of donations.
explanation.definitionFit: Altruists act selflessly for others, so generous givers or patrons are examples.

clue.text: Total of fishes caught for late feast

parts.note: all means the total

indicators.note: caught means heard, so the fish word is taken by its sound

parts.note: soles are flatfish

explanation.surface: The whole catch of fish was landed for a belated banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' means dead, not tardy: All Souls' Day, 2 November, is the church feast commemorating the faithful departed.
explanation.definitionFit: All Souls is the Christian festival honouring the dead, the late, so it is a feast of the departed.

clue.text: Part of plant, one more deficient in oxygen

indicators.note: deficient in means lacking, so the oxygen symbol goes missing

parts.note: another means one more
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A plant part that is one more starved of oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'more deficient' wants to read as one comparative, but 'one more' is the word and 'deficient in' the removal.
explanation.definitionFit: The anther is the pollen-bearing tip of a flower's stamen, a component of the plant.

clue.text: Something to beat line dancing?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tall narrow drum played with the hands
second meaning: a dance done in a long single-file line

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a rhythm to outdo in a dance; the two halves are the drum and the party dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The same Cuban word names both the hand drum and the dance performed by people in a snaking file.

clue.text: Susan Coolidge's girl learned cricket in US

parts.note: Katy Carr is the heroine of Susan Coolidge's novel What Katy Did
did means studied or learned, as in 'did French at school'

explanation.surface: The heroine of an old children's book picked up the American game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cricket' is the insect, not the game: the American katydid is a green bush cricket named for its call.
explanation.definitionFit: A katydid is a North American bush cricket, an insect whose song sounds like its name.

clue.text: Oscar's best mate?

parts.note: Oscar Wilde wrote a comedy with this title; read literally it is the perfect spouse

explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is Wilde, not an award or a friend's name: his 1895 play title describes a perfect partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Wilde's play literally names a perfect spouse, which is what a best mate in marriage would be.

clue.text: Fell over can I dropped, getting notice from landlord?

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the hill word is written backwards

parts.note: a fell is upland moor in northern England

indicators.note: dropped means let fall, so the letter I is taken away

parts.note: can is slang for toilet

explanation.surface: Someone tripped over a can, dropping it, and then got a letter from the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like a past tense; it is the noun for moorland, reversed to give ROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign advertising space for rent is something a landlord puts up, an example of a landlord's notice.

clue.text: Impossible, however you look at it

indicators.note: the phrase reads the same from either end, so it looks identical whichever way it is viewed

parts.note: impossible, and the phrase reads identically both ways

explanation.surface: Something is impossible from every angle.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is not on is informal British for saying it cannot or should not happen.

clue.text: Unlikely worshipper in church in Durham?

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Hindu would hardly be found worshipping in Durham Cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Hinduism would not normally attend a Christian church, so they are an improbable member of that congregation.

clue.text: Earl passed over after working with a single duke?

indicators.note: after says the earl and the passing come after the word for working

parts.note: on means working, as a machine is on
handed over means passed over

explanation.surface: An earl was ignored in favour of a lone duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duke' is slang for a fist or hand (as in 'put up your dukes'), not a nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes is old slang for fists, so having only one of them means using only a single hand.

clue.text: Chaste lady on vacation avoiding excess

parts.note: modest means chaste or decorous

indicators.note: a word on vacation is emptied of its inside, leaving only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A virtuous woman on holiday keeps away from overindulgence.
explanation.definitionFit: To act modestly is to act in a restrained or moderate way, without extravagance.

clue.text: Taking A-road, head west for treeless plain

indicators.note: in an across answer heading west means reading right to left
taking means the head word takes the road letters alongside it

parts.note: A plus RD, the abbreviation for road
nut is slang for head

explanation.surface: A traveller takes the main road and heads west across open country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'west' reverses A RD NUT (head) to give TUNDRA.
explanation.definitionFit: The tundra is the vast flat Arctic region where the subsoil is frozen and trees cannot grow.

clue.text: Pure daughter leaving disco, it's said

parts.note: utter means pure, as in utter nonsense

indicators.note: leaving means going away, so the daughter letter departs

parts.note: a disco is a dance
D is the abbreviation for daughter in family trees

explanation.surface: An innocent girl leaving a nightclub, so the rumour goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An utterance is any spoken word or statement, that is, something which is voiced.

clue.text: A fish by itself derived nutrient from algae

parts.note: a gar is a long-snouted fish
by itself means placed beside a copy of itself, so a fish is repeated

explanation.surface: A lone fish obtained its food from seaweed.
explanation.definitionFit: Agar-agar is a gelatinous substance extracted from red seaweed, used as a culture medium for growing bacteria.

clue.text: Draw attention to lover scratching Nutmeg's back

indicators.note: scratching means striking out, so the setter's reversed letters are removed

parts.note: a mistress is a lover

indicators.note: back means the contraction is read in reverse

parts.note: Nutmeg is the setter, so Nutmeg's is I'm

explanation.surface: A lover scratches the setter's back to get noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: Nutmeg is the clue's setter, so 'Nutmeg's' is I'M; 'back' turns that into MI, which is scratched from MISTRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress a point is to emphasise it, so highlighting is a synonym.

clue.text: Hairband with minor problem

parts.note: the band part gives ring
a let is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A hair accessory with a slight defect.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringlet is a curled lock of hair.

clue.text: Encourage chopper making extension for hatching birds

parts.note: to egg on is to encourage
chopper is slang for tooth

explanation.surface: Urging on a helicopter to build an extension, perhaps an aviary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chopper' suggests a helicopter or an axe; here it is slang for a tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: The egg tooth is a small hard tip on a chick's beak used to crack the shell when hatching.

clue.text: Medic examining pupils?

parts.note: pupils are the openings of the eyes, not schoolchildren, so this is an eye doctor

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a school doctor; the pupils are in the eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: An oculist is an old term for an eye specialist, an ophthalmologist or optometrist.

clue.text: Ancient lawgiver's work pieced together

definitions.meaning: first meaning: of Moses, who gave the Ten Commandments
second meaning: a picture made of small tiles

explanation.walkthrough: The adjective for Moses, as in Mosaic law, is also the noun for a tiled artwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Mosaic is the adjective for things of Moses, and also an artwork assembled from small coloured tiles.

clue.text: Red iron pot in ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed up, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Something red in an iron pot, being ground down.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinot noir is a black grape and the red wine made from it.

clue.text: Metal casing over unknown poison

indicators.note: casing means enclosing, so the metal wraps the other letters

parts.note: tin is a metal
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A metal case holding some mysterious poison.
explanation.definitionFit: A toxin is a poisonous substance, especially one made by a living organism.

clue.text: Thrashes noisy mobs

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a rout is an old word for a disorderly crowd

explanation.walkthrough: The verb for crushing defeats is also an old noun for unruly crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: To rout an enemy is to beat them decisively, and a rout is also a rowdy rabble.

clue.text: Soothe relative with a kiss

parts.note: X is a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Calm a family member down by giving them a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: To relax someone is to calm them or ease their tension.

clue.text: Country area close to region with granite rocks

indicators.note: rocks means shakes, so the letters are rearranged
the close of a word is its end, so the last letter of region

explanation.surface: A country region near an area of granite outcrops.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentina is a nation of South America, an example of a country.

clue.text: Vigorously contest red card, but acknowledge one's error

indicators.note: vigorously suggests the words are shaken up so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A footballer furiously disputes a sending-off but then admits the referee was right.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand corrected is the idiom for conceding you were wrong after being put right.
